readings.title: Up from Slavery: the Indian students at Hampton, and the colour line (Chapter VI)
readings.challenge: Notice where Washington tells a story and where he draws a lesson from it, and test whether each lesson fits its story.
readings.focus: A young Black teacher made “house father” to Native American students, and the strange rules by which America sorted its races.
readings.context: Booker T. Washington (1856–1915) was born enslaved in Virginia, studied at Hampton Institute and in 1881 founded Tuskegee Institute, a school for Black students in Alabama; Up from Slavery (1901) is his autobiography. Hampton, in Virginia, was founded after the Civil War by General Samuel Armstrong to educate freed people. From 1878 it also took Native American students sent from western reservations, under a government policy meant to make them give up their own languages, dress and ways; Washington, invited back to Hampton as a young teacher, was put in charge of their building. Frederick Douglass (about 1818–1895) escaped slavery to become the great abolitionist speaker. Caste is a fixed rank by birth; the colour line is the boundary between races drawn by law and custom. Washington writes “Negro” and “coloured,” the respectful words of his time. It is read on Columbus Day, kept in many places also as Indigenous Peoples’ Day, because it shows the meeting of peoples begun in 1492 as it stood four centuries later.
readings.contentNote: Washington uses the period’s words for Native Americans (“wild,” “perfectly ignorant,” “red men”) and describes, largely with approval, a schooling that made them cut their hair and give up their blankets and language. He recounts racial segregation on trains, a steamboat and a hotel, and a town close to a lynching.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, from General Armstrong’s experiment of educating Indians at Hampton through the traveller from Morocco; opens “About this time the experiment was being tried for the first time, by General Armstrong,…”; closes “…cause of the excitement, though, found it prudent after that not to speak English.”.

questions.prompt: What did Washington fear when he moved into the Indian students’ building, and what did he find?
facilitatorNotes: He doubted he could succeed: he believed the Indian students felt themselves above white people and “far above the Negro,” who had “submitted to slavery,” and most people expected the experiment to fail. He found them “about like any other human beings,” won their confidence, love and respect, and saw them plan to add to his comfort.
evidence: I found that they were about like any other human beings; that they responded to kind treatment and resented ill-treatment.

questions.prompt: Washington lists what the students “disliked most,” then turns on what “no white American” can accept. What is he criticising, and does his own job at Hampton fit his criticism?
facilitatorNotes: He mocks the belief that another race is civilised only when it wears the white man’s clothes, eats his food, speaks his language and professes his religion. Yet he was hired to run that very programme, and he praises the Black students for teaching the Indians English and “civilized habits.” One reading: a careful criticism made from inside the system. Another: a tension he does not resolve. Students should cite both sentences.
evidence: The things that they disliked most, I think, were to have their long hair cut, to give up wearing their blankets, and to cease smoking
no white American ever thinks that any other race is wholly civilized until he wears the white man's clothes

questions.prompt: Douglass in the baggage-car, the conductor, and George Washington lifting his hat: what do these stories share? Who, according to them, is degraded by prejudice?
facilitatorNotes: Each moves the shame from the person excluded to the person who excludes. Douglass says the degradation falls on “those who are inflicting it”; George Washington will not let a poor man be politer than he; the conductor peering at a passenger’s feet makes the colour line absurd. Washington draws the lesson: a gentleman is tested by how he treats those less fortunate.
evidence: They cannot degrade Frederick Douglass.
Do you suppose that I am going to permit a poor, ignorant, coloured man to be more polite than I am?

questions.prompt: On the steamboat and at the hotel, the Indian could be served but Washington could not. Why does he call this “the curious workings of caste”? What does the man from Morocco add?
facilitatorNotes: The two were “of about the same complexion,” so the rule was not about skin but about being an American Negro, a descendant of the enslaved. The Moroccan traveller was accepted once he was known to be a foreigner, and wisely stopped speaking English. Washington’s dry phrases (the steward “seemed to be an expert”) carry his judgment without open anger.
evidence: since the Indian and I were of about the same complexion
found it prudent after that not to speak English

questions.prompt: Washington tells several painful stories as jokes (“That will settle it”). What does humour let him do for his readers in 1901, and what might it cost?
facilitatorNotes: It lets him expose the absurdity of the colour line without accusing his mostly white readers, so they keep listening; he was famous for conciliation. The cost: congratulating himself that his race did not lose “one of its members” makes light of a real humiliation, and critics then and since found his tone too accommodating. Either view can be defended from the passage.
evidence: I congratulated myself that my race was fortunate in not losing one of its members.
a rather amusing instance

readings.title: Up from Slavery: a first Thanksgiving, and a dining room dug by hand (Chapter X, end)
readings.challenge: Follow how Washington turns a story of hardship into one of gratitude, and decide whether you believe him.
readings.focus: Money raised in the North, a first Thanksgiving in an unfinished building, and a boarding department begun with nothing.
readings.context: Booker T. Washington (1856–1915) was born enslaved in Virginia, studied at Hampton Institute and in 1881 founded Tuskegee Institute, a school for Black students in Alabama; Up from Slavery (1901) is his autobiography. Tuskegee opened in 1881 in a church and a shanty with no land or buildings of its own; Porter Hall, its first building, was put up partly by the students’ own labour. Miss Olivia Davidson was a teacher who helped Washington found the school and later became his wife. Northampton is a town in Massachusetts. A boarding department houses and feeds students who live at the school; “the Master” is Jesus. The reading falls on Thanksgiving because it tells of the first Thanksgiving service the people of Tuskegee had ever kept.

excerpt.locator: Chapter X, from the summer of 1882 in the North to the end of the chapter; opens “In the summer of 1882 Miss Davidson and I both went North and engaged in the work of…”; closes “…as we did, and built ourselves up year by year, by a slow and natural process of growth.”.

questions.prompt: What did the missionary officer in New York advise Washington to do, and what happened in Northampton? What do the two stories have in common?
facilitatorNotes: The officer refused a letter and told him to go home, sure he would raise no more than his travelling expenses; Washington thanked him and went on. In Northampton he spent half a day looking for a coloured family to board with, “never dreaming” a hotel would take him, and was surprised to be accommodated. Both show low expectations, others’ and his own, proved wrong.
evidence: I thanked him for his advice, and proceeded on my journey.
never dreaming that any hotel would admit me

questions.prompt: Why was that Thanksgiving “a day of Thanksgiving for them never to be forgotten”? What were the people thankful for?
facilitatorNotes: It was the first service of its kind they had ever observed, held in the chapel of their own new building, though it was not finished; and a stranger, Mr. Bedford, had gladly come to preach. They gave thanks for something they had begun to build themselves.
evidence: It was the first service of the kind that the coloured people there had ever observed
The sight of the new building made it a day of Thanksgiving for them never to be forgotten.

questions.prompt: In the middle of a story about buildings and meals, Washington stops to describe Mr. Bedford and Mr. Logan. Why might he include them here?
facilitatorNotes: Thanksgiving is also gratitude to people. Both men model what he values: Bedford “completely obliterates himself” and seeks the least attractive service; Logan’s “patience and faith” never left him. Their steady service, not money alone, built the school. Some readers also note that naming them honours the school’s friends before a public of donors.
evidence: He completely obliterates himself in everything
his patience and faith in our ultimate success have not left him

questions.prompt: List what went wrong in the boarding department’s first weeks. Which remark came nearest to discouraging Washington, and why that one?
facilitatorNotes: No kitchen or dining room, so students dug out a dark basement; cooking outdoors in pots over a fire; carpenters’ benches for tables; almost no dishes; meals at no fixed hour, with meat burnt, bread unsalted, tea forgotten; boys taking turns for one coffee-cup. The girl at the well with its broken rope said, “We can’t even get water to drink at this school.” It hurt because it was a student’s honest verdict on the whole school, overheard.
evidence: We can't even get water to drink at this school.
I think no one remark ever came so near discouraging me as that one.

questions.prompt: “I am glad that we had it.” Why is Washington glad of the hardships? Is his reasoning convincing?
facilitatorNotes: Doing it themselves gave them “a foundation which one has made for one’s self” and kept them from becoming “stuck up”; growth came “by a slow and natural process.” A defensible view: the gratitude is earned, since the students’ own labour made the school theirs. Another: hindsight makes hardship look useful, the hungry girl at the well might not have been glad, and the lesson in thrift also suited the donors Washington wrote for.
evidence: As I look back now over that part of our struggle, I am glad that we had it.
It means a great deal, I think, to start off on a foundation which one has made for one's self.

readings.title: Up from Slavery: the Shaw Memorial and the old flag (Chapter XV)
readings.challenge: Compare what Washington tells in his own voice with what he lets a newspaper say for him.
readings.focus: A monument to a white colonel and his Black regiment, dedicated in Boston in 1897, and the moment a wounded veteran raised the flag.
readings.context: Booker T. Washington (1856–1915) was born enslaved in Virginia, studied at Hampton Institute and in 1881 founded Tuskegee Institute, a school for Black students in Alabama; Up from Slavery (1901) is his autobiography. Robert Gould Shaw (1837–1863), a young white officer from a Boston anti-slavery family, commanded the 54th Massachusetts, one of the first Black regiments raised in the North in the Civil War; he and many of his men were killed leading the assault on Fort Wagner, near Charleston, South Carolina, in July 1863. Augustus Saint-Gaudens’s bronze memorial to Shaw and the regiment was dedicated on Boston Common on 31 May 1897. Sergeant William H. Carney, wounded several times while carrying the flag at Fort Wagner, later received the Medal of Honor. John Andrew was the wartime governor who raised the regiment, and George Stearns recruited for it. “Mine eyes have seen the glory” opens the Battle Hymn of the Republic. The report Washington quotes runs from “The core and kernel” to the three cheers. It is read on Memorial Day, kept since the Civil War for those who died in the nation’s wars.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XV, from the invitation to dedicate the Robert Gould Shaw monument through the audience’s response to Sergeant Carney’s flag; opens “Early in the year 1897 I received a letter inviting me to deliver an address at the…”; closes “…this. For a number of minutes the audience seemed to entirely lose control of itself.”.

questions.prompt: Washington hands most of this account to a newspaper report. Why might he let the Boston Transcript describe the meeting instead of describing it himself?
facilitatorNotes: He says the report will describe it better than he could. It also lets him include praise of himself (“the superb address”) that he could not decently write, and an outside witness is more convincing to readers. Some readers see modesty; others a shrewd way to have the praise and keep the modesty.
evidence: will describe it better than any words of mine could do
the superb address of the Negro President of Tuskegee

questions.prompt: According to the report, what did Washington’s presence mean to the Boston audience? Find two phrases.
facilitatorNotes: He was “the civic justification of the old abolition spirit,” “the proof of her ancient and indomitable faith,” “the crown and glory of the old war days.” To the old anti-slavery families he proved that the war and its losses had been worth it.
evidence: the civic justification of the old abolition spirit of Massachusetts
the crown and glory of the old war days of suffering and strife

questions.prompt: Washington tells the veterans, “your commander is not dead.” What monument does he say Shaw has besides the bronze one?
facilitatorNotes: The surviving soldiers and the “loyal race” they represent: people living out what Shaw died for make a monument “which time could not wear away.” Even without Boston’s statue or history’s record, Shaw would be remembered in them.
evidence: to you, your commander is not dead
Robert Gould Shaw would have a monument which time could not wear away

questions.prompt: Why did Sergeant Carney’s rising with the flag move the audience more than any speech? What might “The old flag never touched the ground” mean in 1897, thirty-four years after Fort Wagner?
facilitatorNotes: It was unplanned, “as if by instinct,” and it was the same man with the same flag: the past standing up in the room. His words say that Black soldiers kept faith with the nation when it mattered most. In 1897, as segregation spread in the South, they can also be heard as a reminder of what the nation owed them in return. Either reading is defensible.
evidence: he rose, as if by instinct, and raised the flag
The old flag never touched the ground.

questions.prompt: Memorial Day honours the dead. Whom does this ceremony honour most, the dead or the living? Use the speech and the scene.
facilitatorNotes: Both, but the climax belongs to the living: the “scarred and scattered remnants” with empty sleeves, and Carney with his flag. Washington’s speech moves honour from the bronze figure to living people, saying the soldiers and their race are Shaw’s true monument. Others argue the living are honoured only as witnesses to the dead, whose sacrifice the whole day is about.
evidence: to the scarred and scattered remnants of the Fifty-fourth
Though Boston erected no monument and history recorded no story
